title: Why is there suffering?
hookLine: Christians have wrestled with this for millennia and offered no easy answer

lines: A BEDSIDE, THE NEWS, A FUNERAL.
IF GOD IS GOOD, WHY THIS?
cards: "O LORD, how long shall I cry, and thou wilt not hear!" That isn't a skeptic in a debate hall. It's a prophet, Habakkuk, in the opening lines of his book, watching violence and injustice go on while heaven seems quiet.
The same question turns up at hospital bedsides, in the late news, at a funeral for someone who died far too young. If God is good, and God is strong, why this?
A new block begins, on suffering, doubt and the hardest questions.

teach.h: THEODICY: GOD'S GOODNESS, THE WORLD'S PAIN.
teach.b: Today's word is theodicy: the name philosophers and theologians give to any attempt to show that God is good in a world full of pain. God is good. God is powerful.
Terrible things happen, and something seems to have to give.
In Luke, people bring Jesus news of Galileans killed by Pilate, and Jesus raises a second disaster himself: a tower in Siloam fell and killed eighteen people.

"Think ye that they were sinners above all men that dwelt in Jerusalem?" No, he says. In John, his disciples pass a man born blind: "Master, who did sin, this man, or his parents, that he was born blind?"
Jesus: "Neither hath this man sinned, nor his parents." Twice he refuses the neat equation: you suffer, so you must have done something. Christians have offered answers anyway.

teach.h: FREEDOM, FIRE, THE END OF THE STORY.
teach.b: Some say God gave people real freedom, and freedom can wound. Some say suffering can refine a person, the way fire tests gold, a picture Peter's first letter uses for faith.
Some point to Revelation: "And God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; and there shall be no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying, neither shall there be any more pain."
And some say the honest thing: we don't know. Some who have sat with deep suffering warn that an answer wise in a classroom can sound cheap at a bedside.

teach.h: NOT NO ANSWERS. NO EASY ONES.
teach.b: No easy answers, but not no answers: Christians do say God is good, and with those who suffer. The days ahead hold that beside the question.
If you ever feel in danger, in the US you can call or text 988, or reach local emergency help.

how: Christians bring the question of suffering to prayer, to Scripture, especially Job, the Psalms and the cross, and to pastors and friends; churches hold different explanations side by side, and some sit with the question rather than settle it.

o: any attempt to show God is good despite suffering
the study of how God made the world in the beginning
a prayer asking God to end a time of suffering

p: the disciples, about the man born blind
the end of the story, in Revelation

s: Jesus taught that the people killed by the tower of Siloam were worse sinners
"think ye that they were sinners above all men...?" he says no.
a prophet in the Bible asks God how long
Habakkuk: "O LORD, how long shall I cry, and thou wilt not hear!"
Christians give one single answer to suffering
some point to freedom, some to refining fire, some to the end of the story, and some say we don't know.

games.q: you're one of the disciples, walking past a man born blind. you've heard people say that suffering means somebody sinned. what do you ask Jesus?
o: whose sin caused this: his, or his parents'?
games.why: they ask who sinned. Jesus says: "Neither hath this man sinned, nor his parents." he refuses the neat equation.

practice: Bring to mind one piece of suffering you can't make sense of, your own, someone else's, or far away, and hold it the way you'd hold someone's hand, without solving it or arguing it away. When a quick answer pops up, set it down.
If you pray, you can bring it to God the way Habakkuk did, how long; if you don't, let the question be asked into the quiet, and leave it open.

wordCard.voice: Theodicy. Any attempt to show that God is good when the world is full of suffering.

carryVoice: Your line: no easy answers. The question is allowed to stay open here. See you tomorrow.
